Aijeleth Shahar
EYE-eh-leth SHAH-har
noun
Hebrew ayyeleth ha-shachar, “the hind of the morning” or “the deer of the dawn” (ayyeleth, a hind; shachar, dawn, morning); the tune or theme set over the twenty-second psalm, the great psalm of the cross.

📖 Biblical Definition

Aijeleth Shahar, “the hind of the morning,” stands over the twenty-second psalm (Psa 22, title), the most piercing of all the messianic psalms. Whether it names an old melody to which the psalm was set, or a figure of its theme, the image is fitting beyond measure: the gentle hind run down by its hunters at break of day is the suffering Saviour, hunted to death in the dark night of the cross and rising in the morning of resurrection. For this psalm opens with the very cry our Lord uttered upon the tree: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Psa 22:1), which Matthew records from His own lips (Mat 27:46). It foretells, a thousand years before Calvary, the mocking of the bystanders, the piercing of His hands and His feet, and the parting of His garments by lot: “they pierced my hands and my feet” (Psa 22:16). David never suffered these things; the Spirit spoke through him of Great David’s greater Son. And the psalm that begins in forsaking ends in a worldwide kingdom: “all the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD” (Psa 22:27). The hind of the morning is hunted at dusk that a multitude no man can number may rejoice at dawn.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

“The hind of the morning”; the title over the twenty-second psalm, picturing the hunted, suffering, and risen Christ.

AIJELETH SHAHAR, a Hebrew phrase signifying “the hind of the morning” or “the deer of the dawn.”

It stands over the twenty-second psalm, the great psalm of the crucifixion.

Whether a tune-name or a figure of the theme, it pictures the gentle hind hunted at daybreak.

The image befits the suffering Christ, run down to death and rising in the morning.

The psalm foretells the cross a thousand years before it came to pass.

📖 Key Scripture

Psa 22, title — "To the chief Musician upon Aijeleth Shahar, A Psalm of David."

Psa 22:1 — "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?"

Psa 22:16 — "For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet."

Mat 27:46 — "And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The crucifixion psalm; the entry faces no postmodern redefinition, but the critical denial that Psalm 22 is true prophecy of Christ must be answered from the Gospels themselves.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to name is the modern critical insistence that the twenty-second psalm describes only David’s own distress, the pierced hands and parted garments dismissed as poetic exaggeration or read away by altering the text. By that account the most exact prophecy of the cross in all the Old Testament becomes a coincidence, and the agreement with Calvary an accident.

The principle to recover is that the Spirit who inspired the psalm fulfilled it to the letter. Our Lord took its opening cry upon His own lips; the evangelists record the mocking, the lots cast for His vesture, and the piercing, in the very words of David’s song. David did not have his hands and feet pierced; the hind of the morning is Christ, and the psalm is His. To read it otherwise is to be ashamed of the plainest prophecy of the cross.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew for “the hind of the morning,” Aijeleth Shahar titles the twenty-second psalm, the prophecy of the hunted, crucified, and risen Christ.

Aijeleth Shahar — Hebrew ayyeleth ha-shachar, “the hind of the morning.”
